title: 22. Interview: Why Cache?
summary: Interview Q&A for Why Cache? — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Why Cache? interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the memory hierarchy, and why does it justify caching?
**Answer:** The memory hierarchy is the ordered set of storage tiers a CPU or service can reach, each slower and larger than the last: CPU registers (~0.3 ns), L1/L2/L3 SRAM caches (~1–12 ns), DRAM (~100 ns), SSD (~100 μs), HDD (~10 ms), and networked storage across datacenters (~30 ms). Each tier is roughly 10×–1000× slower than the one above it, so moving hot data up the pyramid yields disproportionate latency wins. Caching is the deliberate promotion of frequently accessed data from a slow tier (disk, network) to a fast tier (RAM, edge). Because 99% of reads often touch 1% of data (the Pareto principle applied to access patterns), a small cache in front of a large database eliminates the overwhelming majority of slow reads while keeping cost bounded by cache size rather than total dataset size.
**Visual:**
```
Reg -> L1 -> L2 -> L3 -> RAM -> SSD -> HDD -> Net
0.3ns  1ns   4ns  12ns  100ns  100us  10ms  30ms
                each step ~10x slower
```

### Q2. How does caching reduce database load, and what is the relationship between hit rate and DB QPS?
**Answer:** Every cache hit is a database read avoided. If the cache sits in front of a database and serves a fraction `h` of reads (the hit rate), the database only sees `(1 - h)` of the incoming read traffic. At a 90% hit rate the database load is reduced 10×; at 99% it is reduced 100×; at 99.9% it is reduced 1000×. The math is multiplicative: `db_qps = total_qps × (1 - h)`. This is why even a modest hit rate is hugely valuable — a service that needs to serve 100,000 reads/sec but only achieves 99% cache hits needs its database to handle just 1,000 qps, well within the comfort zone of a single Postgres instance. Amazon's product detail page exploits this: DynamoDB only sees the small fraction of misses that escape the multi-tier CDN + EVCache stack.
**Visual:**
```
Total reads: 100,000 qps
Cache hit rate h = 99%  -->  cache absorbs 99,000 qps
                          -->  DB sees only 1,000 qps (100x reduction)

h=0.90 -> DB sees 10,000 qps (10x)
h=0.99 -> DB sees 1,000  qps (100x)
h=0.999-> DB sees 100    qps (1000x)
```

### Q3. What are the three primary motivations for introducing a cache, and how do they trade off against each other?
**Answer:** The three motivations are latency reduction (sub-ms reads instead of disk-bound ms reads), database load reduction (the DB sees only misses), and cost savings (a small RAM footprint replaces a much larger disk-provisioned database). They reinforce each other: lower latency improves user experience, lower DB load improves reliability under spike, and lower cost lets the business re-invest. The trade-offs are staleness (the cache can lag the source of truth by the TTL), consistency (write-through is consistent but slow; cache-aside is fast but races on invalidation), and complexity (cache is one more distributed system to operate, monitor, and fail over). A 99% hit rate also means a 100× amplification of any thundering-herd or stampede scenario when a hot key expires. The art is choosing TTL, eviction policy, and write strategy so that latency/load/cost wins outweigh the staleness/complexity costs for the specific workload.
**Visual:**
```
Wins                       Costs
+-------------------+      +--------------------+
| latency  -100x    |      | staleness   +TTL   |
| DB load  -100x    | <--  | consistency races  |
| cost     -10x     |      | ops complexity +1  |
+-------------------+      +--------------------+
```

### Q4. Why is the CPU cache (L1/L2/L3) also called a cache, and how is it different from an application-level cache like Redis?
**Answer:** Both are caches in the same fundamental sense: a small, fast storage layer sitting between a slow producer and a fast consumer, exploiting the principle of locality (temporal — recently-used data will be used again; spatial — nearby data will be used together). The CPU cache is hardware-managed, transparent to software, and lives on the same die as the processor — it caches memory lines, automatically evicted via hardware LRU/MESI protocols. An application cache like Redis is software-managed, explicit (the application calls `GET`/`SET`), and lives on a separate machine reached over the network — it caches application objects, evicted via software LRU/LFU/TTL. The CPU cache is命中 or miss at the hardware level; an application cache hits or misses at the protocol level. Both obey the same access-pattern economics: hot data benefits disproportionately, cold data wastes capacity.
**Visual:**
```
Hardware cache (CPU)            Application cache (Redis)
+----------------+              +----------------+
| L1/L2/L3 SRAM  |              | Redis process  |
| hardware mgmt  |              | software mgmt  |
| transparent    |              | explicit GET/SET|
| same die, <1ns |              | network, <1ms  |
| caches lines   |              | caches objects |
+----------------+              +----------------+
        both: locality of reference (temporal + spatial)
```

### Q5. What is the Pareto principle's role in cache effectiveness, and when does caching fail to help?
**Answer:** Most real-world access distributions are heavily skewed — a small fraction of objects accounts for the majority of accesses (the "80/20 rule," often closer to "1% of keys = 50% of traffic"). This skew is what makes caching economical: a small cache that holds the hot 1% can absorb the bulk of reads, yielding a high hit rate without caching the entire dataset. Caching fails to help when access is uniform random (every key is equally likely, so the cache must hold the entire dataset to be useful — no savings), when the working set exceeds available RAM (eviction thrashing, hit rate collapses), when reads are rare and writes dominate (cache amortization never pays off the write-invalidation cost), or when freshness requirements force TTLs so short that misses dominate. Netflix's recommendation cache works because each user's row is hot for that user; a uniform-random analytics query over the full historical table would not benefit from the same cache.
**Visual:**
```
Skewed access (cacheable):       Uniform access (not cacheable):
keys  accesses                   keys  accesses
top 1%   50%  <-- cache these    all keys ~1/N
next 9%  30%                     --> must cache everything
rest 90% 20%  <-- cold           --> no win
hit rate with 1% cache = 50%     hit rate with 1% cache = 1%
```

### Q6. How does the database's own buffer pool relate to an external application cache like Redis?
**Answer:** Both are caches, but they sit at different layers and serve different purposes. The DB buffer pool (PostgreSQL `shared_buffers`, InnoDB `innodb_buffer_pool`) caches disk pages in the database process's RAM — it is page-granular, transparent to the application, and tuned to reduce disk I/O for whatever the database is asked to do. An external application cache like Redis caches application objects (a deserialized user profile, a JSON blob, a computed recommendation), at the granularity the application chooses, with TTLs and eviction the application controls. The DB buffer pool helps even queries that miss the application cache (the disk read may still hit the buffer pool), but it cannot help with cross-network latency or with object deserialization cost — both of which the application cache eliminates. The two are complementary: the application cache short-circuits most reads before they reach the DB; the buffer pool makes the misses that remain fast.
**Visual:**
```
App ---miss---> Redis ---miss---> DB process ---buffer pool---> SSD
                 <1 ms             <1 ms (warm)                  100 us-10 ms
                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                                  DB's own cache, transparent
```

### Q7. What is a cache stampede (thundering herd), and at a high level how is it mitigated?
**Answer:** A cache stampede occurs when a popular key expires (or is evicted) and many concurrent requests simultaneously miss the cache, all reach through to the database, and the resulting load spike knocks the database over — even though a single read would have sufficed to refresh the cache. The herd amplifies a single miss into thousands of identical expensive queries. Mitigations include: **request coalescing** (only one request fetches; others wait for its result), **lock-based mutex** (the first miss acquires a lock, fetches, and populates; concurrent requests wait or serve stale), **early refresh / refresh-ahead** (renew the cache slightly before expiry so it never visibly expires), **TTL jitter** (add random ±10% to TTLs so they don't all expire together), **stale-while-revalidate** (serve the stale value while refreshing in the background), and **probabilistic early expiration** (XFetch algorithm — each request probabilistically refreshes as TTL approaches zero). Netflix's EVCache implements request coalescing and probabilistic early expiration precisely to prevent stampedes on popular profile keys during peak hours.
**Visual:**
```
Without coalescing:            With coalescing:
TTL expires                    TTL expires
   | 1000 requests                | 1 request fetches
   v all miss                      v refreshes cache
+---+---+---+                   +----+----+----+
|DB |DB |DB |                   |wait|wait|wait|
+---+---+---+                   +----+----+----+
   | DB overloaded                  | DB sees 1 query
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run an e-commerce product-detail page serving 50,000 reads/sec during peak. The Postgres backend handles 5,000 qps max. Design a caching layer.
**Answer:** The DB is the bottleneck at 10× headroom shortage, so caching is mandatory. Compute the required hit rate: `db_qps = 50,000 × (1 - h) ≤ 5,000` → `h ≥ 0.90`. A 90% hit rate suffices on paper, but for spike resilience and to leave DB headroom for writes, target 95–99%. Introduce a Redis cluster (3 shards × 1 master + 1 replica each, hash-slot sharding) co-located with the application tier for sub-millisecond reads. Use a cache-aside pattern: read Redis, on miss read Postgres and back-fill Redis with a 5-minute TTL. Add TTL jitter (±60 s) to avoid synchronized expiry. For popular keys (e.g., a flash-sale product), implement request coalescing via a per-key mutex to prevent stampede. Set up Prometheus alerts on hit rate (page if <90%), eviction rate, and p99 cache latency. Finally, run a chaos drill that kills one Redis shard — the application must fall through to Postgres and the DB must survive the temporary hit-rate drop, validating the design's blast radius.
**Visual:**
```
50,000 rps
   |
   v
+-----------+   hit 95%   +----------+
| Redis x3  |------------>| Response |
+-----------+             +----------+
   | miss 5% (2,500 rps)
   v
+-----------+
| Postgres  |   <-- capacity 5,000 rps, headroom 2x
+-----------+
```

### Q2. Netflix wants to cache user playback profiles for 200M subscribers. Each profile is 2 KB. How big should the cache be, and what hit rate should you target?
**Answer:** Total dataset size = 200M × 2 KB = 400 GB. Caching everything in RAM is feasible but expensive; instead, exploit skew: the active-user base at any moment is much smaller (say 20M concurrent streams), and within that, the recent-active set is even smaller. Size the cache for the top 5% of users = 10M profiles × 2 KB = 20 GB per region — comfortably fits on 3–4 large Redis nodes. Target a 99% hit rate so the recommendation backend is rarely touched. Replicate across regions (us-east, us-west, eu-west, ap-southeast) so each region's cache serves local users; cross-region misses fall through to the central profile service. Use TTL = 24 h with refresh-ahead so active users never see expiry; inactive users naturally evict via LRU. Track hit rate per region — if eu-west drops below 99%, scale that region's cache up. Netflix's actual EVCache deployment uses roughly this design: hundreds of memcached nodes per region, 99%+ hit rate, sub-millisecond profile reads.
**Visual:**
```
200M users x 2 KB = 400 GB total
Cache top 5% = 10M x 2 KB = 20 GB / region
3-4 Redis nodes per region
Hit rate target: 99% (DB sees <1% of reads)

[us-east] [us-west] [eu-west] [ap-SE]  <-- regional caches
     \       |        /        /
      \      |       /        /
       +-----------+
       | Profile   |  <-- central source of truth (miss path)
       | Service   |
       +-----------+
```

### Q3. Amazon's product detail page must render in under 200 ms end-to-end. The catalog DB averages 30 ms per query and you need 8 queries per page. Can you meet the SLO without caching?
**Answer:** Without caching, the page would take 8 × 30 ms = 240 ms in DB time alone, plus service overhead — already over the 200 ms budget before accounting for network hops, serialization, or any other work. So no, the SLO cannot be met without caching. Introduce a Redis layer: each of the 8 lookups becomes ~0.5 ms on a hit, so cache-hit pages render in 8 × 0.5 ms = 4 ms of cache time plus service overhead — comfortably under budget. For misses (assume 5% miss rate, ~0.4 misses per page), one DB query at 30 ms still leaves the page well under 200 ms. Cache product data with a 5-minute TTL (prices change infrequently), inventory with a 30-second TTL (more dynamic), and user-personalized recommendations with a 60-second TTL. Use a CDN edge cache for the fully-rendered anonymous page (no user personalization) so most requests terminate at the edge — Amazon does exactly this, with CloudFront terminating the majority of anonymous product-page reads.
**Visual:**
```
Without cache:  8 queries x 30 ms = 240 ms  --> SLO FAIL
With Redis:     8 hits x 0.5 ms = 4 ms      --> 4 ms + overhead ~ 50 ms  --> SLO PASS
                miss scenario: 1 DB hit + 7 cache hits = 30 + 3.5 = 33.5 ms --> SLO PASS
```

### Q4. WhatsApp caches last-seen timestamps for billions of users to render read receipts. The dataset is 50 GB; Cassandra handles the source of truth. Should you cache, and how?
**Answer:** Yes — caching is essential because read receipts are read far more often than written (each message-send triggers reads of every participant's last-seen, but a user's last-seen only updates when they actually open the app — a 1000:1 read:write ratio). Caching 50 GB of last-seen timestamps in Redis across a small cluster (5–6 nodes) eliminates 99%+ of Cassandra reads, which would otherwise need a full partition lookup per send. Use a cache-aside pattern: on message-send, batch-`MGET` the last-seen of all recipients; on miss, fall through to Cassandra and back-fill. Set TTL = 5 minutes (last-seen older than 5 minutes is functionally the same as "online recently"). Writes (when a user opens the app) update Cassandra and invalidate the cache key so the next read sees fresh data. Cache size is bounded by the active-user set, not total registrations — most registered users are inactive, so 50 GB theoretical fits in ~5 GB of actual hot data.
**Visual:**
```
On message-send to group of 10:
  MGET lastseen:user1..user10  (1 Redis roundtrip, ~0.5 ms)
    9 hits + 1 miss:
      miss -> Cassandra SELECT (5 ms) -> backfill Redis
  Result: 1 cache miss, 9 hits, 1 DB query instead of 10
```

### Q5. YouTube's video metadata page gets 1B views/day. Caching seems obvious, but what are the failure modes, and how do you mitigate them?
**Answer:** Failure modes include: (1) **cache stampede** when a viral video's metadata key expires and millions of concurrent viewers miss — mitigate with request coalescing and probabilistic early refresh. (2) **Hot-key concentration** — a single MrBeast video may get 10M views/hour, all hashing to one Redis shard — mitigate with hot-key replication (write the same key to multiple shards, read round-robin) or with a small in-process L1 cache in each application server. (3) **Cache OOM** if too many keys accumulate — use LRU eviction and size the cluster for 80% utilization. (4) **Stale metadata after edits** — title/description changes must invalidate the cache, but invalidation can race with reads; mitigate with versioned keys (`video:42:v7`) or short TTLs on mutable fields. (5) **Cache failure** — if Redis dies, all reads fall through to the metadata DB; mitigate with multi-AZ Redis replicas and a circuit breaker that serves stale data instead of erroring. YouTube uses a multi-tier cache (browser → CDN edge → regional memcached → storage backend) so each failure mode is absorbed by the tier above.
**Visual:**
```
Viral video -> hot key on one shard:
  +-----+-----+-----+
  | S1  | S2  | S3  |
  +-----+-----+-----+
    ^^^
    99% of traffic -> S1 overloaded

Mitigation: hot-key replication
  video:42 -> written to S1, S2, S3
  reads round-robin across all 3
  load spread 3x
```

### Q6. Uber's surge pricing updates every minute. Caching surge multipliers seems risky — won't users see stale prices? How do you cache safely?
**Answer:** Surge pricing has two conflicting constraints: freshness (a stale 1.5× multiplier when the true value is 2.5× loses revenue and misleads drivers) and latency (every ride request must read the multiplier in under 10 ms). Solve this with a short-TTL cache (e.g., 30 seconds) plus refresh-ahead: a background worker recomputes surge every minute and writes to Redis, so the cache never expires from the read path's perspective — readers always see the latest computed value. Use a write-through pattern: when the surge recomputation job finishes, it writes both to the source-of-truth store and to Redis atomically. For in-flight ride requests, accept the eventual consistency: a 30-second-old surge value is fine because pricing is approximate by nature (it changes continuously anyway). For the actual fare charged at ride completion, re-read from the source of truth, not the cache — so any drift during the ride is corrected at settlement. This is the standard pattern for any "frequently read, periodically recomputed" value.
**Visual:**
```
Surge recompute job (every 60s):
  compute -> write DB + write Redis (write-through)

Read path (every ride request):
  GET surge:zone42 -> Redis (0.5 ms)
  (always a hit because refresh-ahead keeps it warm)

Settlement (ride ends):
  read DB (source of truth) -> final fare
  (cache may have drifted, settlement corrects)
```

### Q7. Instagram wants to add a cache in front of Cassandra to reduce read load. The team says "Redis is faster, just add it." What questions do you ask before approving?
**Answer:** Before approving, I'd ask: (1) What's the current Cassandra read latency and QPS? If Cassandra is already at 5 ms p99 with 80% CPU, a cache helps; if it's at 1 ms with 20% CPU, the cache adds complexity for no win. (2) What's the read:write ratio? Caching write-heavy workloads (less than 5:1 read:write) rarely pays off because every write must invalidate the cache, eliminating the read savings. (3) What's the access skew? Uniform-random access doesn't cache well; skew is required. (4) What's the consistency requirement? If readers must see writes immediately, cache-aside introduces races; write-through or versioned keys may be needed. (5) What's the working set size? If hot data exceeds comfortable RAM (say >50 GB), the cache may thrash. (6) What's the cache failure plan? If Redis dies, can Cassandra absorb the full read load temporarily? (7) Who operates the cache, and how is it monitored (hit rate, eviction, latency, memory)? (8) Is there a simpler option — Cassandra's own row cache, or a materialized view, or read replicas? If yes, prefer the simpler path before introducing a new distributed system. Only after these answers favor caching should you add Redis.
**Visual:**
```
Decision checklist:
[1] Cassandra already slow?   yes/no
[2] read:write >= 10:1?        yes/no
[3] access skewed?            yes/no
[4] consistency lax (TTL ok)?  yes/no
[5] working set fits in RAM?  yes/no
[6] cache failure plan?       yes/no
[7] ops team ready?           yes/no
[8] simpler options ruled out? yes/no
--> 6+ yes => add cache; otherwise reconsider
```
